lead: Diesel knock is the hard, metallic combustion noise of a CI engine. Its cause is a long ignition delay: fuel keeps arriving while nothing burns, and when ignition finally comes, all of it burns at once in the premixed stage. The pressure jumps steeply, the structure rings and the bearings take a hammer blow. Some syllabi treat diesel knock as a topic of its own, while others fold it into CI combustion; either way, examiners like to ask how it differs from SI knock and how it is controlled.
prereq: You need: the four CI stages and the factors affecting delay (CI combustion), and SI knock (abnormal combustion).

blocks.text: Every CI cycle has a premixed spike; diesel knock is simply that spike grown too large. A long delay lets more fuel into the cylinder before ignition, more of it mixes, and the premixed stage releases a large share of the heat in a few degrees. The rate of pressure rise, not the peak pressure, is what the ear and the bearings feel. A smooth diesel stays near or below about 5 bar/°CA; knocking cycles go well beyond that.

Note the contrast with SI knock. In an SI engine knock comes at the end of combustion, from end gas that ignites too early. In a CI engine knock comes at the start of combustion, from fuel that ignites too late. So what cures one causes the other.

items: Fuel with a higher cetane number, or a cetane improver additive such as an alkyl nitrate: shorter chemical delay.

Hotter, denser air: a higher compression ratio, supercharging, or a hotter intake. At cold start an intake air heater warms the incoming air, while a glow plug heats the air inside the chamber near the spray; both shorten the delay.
Injection timing close to the optimum (about 10° to 15° bTDC), where the air is hottest.
Pilot injection or a low initial injection rate: a small first shot ignites and heats the chamber, so the main shot meets a flame instead of waiting; less fuel collects.
Finer atomisation: high injection pressure and a clean nozzle shorten the physical delay.
Chamber design and air motion: organised swirl and hot surfaces help early mixing and ignition; indirect injection chambers run quieter (see combustion chambers).

examples.question: The engine of the CI chapter (2000 rev/min, injection from 15° bTDC at 1.6 mg/°) runs on two fuels. Fuel A gives a 0.9 ms delay; fuel B, of higher cetane number, gives 0.5 ms. For each, find the delay in degrees, the start of combustion and the fuel injected before ignition. The computed traces in the figure give a steepest rise of 8.8 bar/°CA for A and 6.3 bar/°CA for B. Comment.
steps: Degrees per ms at 2000 rev/min: 0.006 × 2000 = 12 °/ms (the 6 is 360° ÷ 60 s, the 0.001 turns ms into s).
Fuel A: 12 × 0.9 = 10.8°; combustion starts at −15° + 10.8° = 4.2° bTDC; fuel before ignition 1.6 × 10.8 = 17.3 mg.
Fuel B: 12 × 0.5 = 6.0°; combustion starts at −15° + 6° = 9° bTDC; fuel before ignition 1.6 × 6.0 = 9.6 mg.
Fuel B halves the fuel waiting at ignition (9.6 against 17.3 mg), so its premixed spike is smaller and the steepest rise falls from 8.8 to 6.3 bar/°CA.
Fuel B starts burning earlier, so its peak pressure is a little higher (86 against 80 bar) even though it runs more smoothly: peak pressure alone does not measure knock.
examples.answer: A: 10.8°, 4.2° bTDC, 17.3 mg. B: 6.0°, 9° bTDC, 9.6 mg. The higher-cetane fuel cuts the fuel collected before ignition by 45 % and the steepest pressure rise by 29 %.

traps: Diesel knock comes at the start of combustion; SI knock comes at the end. Do not describe diesel knock as end-gas autoignition.
A high compression ratio reduces diesel knock but increases SI knock. Read the question for the engine type.
Judge knock by the rate of pressure rise; a smoother cycle can have a higher peak pressure.
A glow plug heats the chamber air near the injector; it is not an intake air heater.

quiz.a: A long ignition delay: fuel injected during the delay collects and then burns almost all at once in the premixed stage, giving a very steep pressure rise.

quiz.q: Name three methods of controlling diesel knock.
quiz.a: Any three: higher cetane fuel or a cetane improver; higher compression ratio or inlet temperature or boost; injection near the optimum timing; pilot injection; finer atomisation; chamber design with good air motion.

quiz.q: Why is a high-octane fuel a poor diesel fuel?
quiz.a: High octane means the fuel resists autoignition, which gives a long ignition delay in a CI engine and so more diesel knock.

quiz.q: At 1800 rev/min the delay falls from 1.5 ms to 1.1 ms. Find the change in degrees.
With injection at 1.2 mg/° and a delay of 9°, how much fuel collects before ignition?
Explain why the factors that reduce knock in an SI engine increase it in a CI engine.
quiz.a: SI knock needs the end gas to ignite early, so long delays help; CI knock needs the fuel to ignite late, so short delays help. Higher compression, hotter air and walls, and easily ignited fuel shorten the delay: good for CI, bad for SI.

beyond: Modern common-rail diesels hold combustion noise down with one or two pilot shots and closed-loop control from in-cylinder pressure. Low-temperature combustion modes deliberately lengthen the delay to premix the charge for low soot and NOx, and then need very careful control of the pressure rise. Search for combustion noise meters, pilot injection and premixed charge compression ignition.

figure.caption: The worked example’s two fuels in the same diesel: the shorter delay of fuel B lets less fuel collect, so its pressure rises less steeply, even though its earlier start gives a slightly higher peak.

spec.aria: Two computed diesel pressure traces with a dashed motoring curve. Fuel A, delay 0.9 milliseconds, starts burning at 4.2 degrees before TDC, steepest rise 8.8 bar per degree, peak 80 bar. Fuel B, delay 0.5 milliseconds, starts at 9 degrees before TDC, steepest rise 6.3 bar per degree, peak 86 bar.
